title: Soil mid-infrared spectroscopy
text: This course takes soil mid-infrared spectroscopy and rebuilds it inside R’s tidyverse and tidymodels. You’ll load real spectrometer output and engineer features from it. Then you’ll catch bad samples, fit and score a model, and run the same pipeline on a public global spectral library.

title: Soil mid-infrared spectroscopy
text:
Why tidyverse and tidymodels
Soil MIR spectroscopy already has capable, purpose-built R packages: prospectr and resemble, among others, cover preprocessing and spectral similarity in real depth. This course proposes an alternative: wrap that domain-specific work inside the tidyverse and tidymodels, the general frameworks most R users already know.
For me, four things make tidyverse and tidymodels worth building this course on.

The abstractions read naturally. recipe(), mutate(), step_snv(), each one names what it does. That keeps your attention on the domain instead of on R itself while modelling. Knowing what’s underneath still matters. This course spends real time unpacking it. But during modelling, the abstractions keep your attention on the pipeline rather than the implementation.
tidymodels also provides a harness for modelling and validating rigorously: splitting, resampling, tuning, and evaluation all follow the same structure, one that’s easy to get wrong by hand. A pipeline built this way is reproducible and repeatable.
Build it once, reuse it again and again, on a new dataset, a new target, a colleague’s laptop.
And building on tidyverse and tidymodels means building on a vast, expressive, mainstream ecosystem, one this course borrows rather than reinvents.

Base recipes ships no steps for spectra. This course adds a handful, wrapping prospectr and resemble underneath. 4-feature-engineering.qmd tells that story properly. Everything downstream of them is standard tidymodels. We won’t reteach the tidyverse’s own documentation, its books, or its cheatsheets. Where this course points at a reference instead of re-explaining it, follow the link. That reference will outlast this course.

title: Soil mid-infrared spectroscopy
text:
How this course teaches
Each page runs top-down. It opens with the full step at the level you’d actually use day to day, one function call that returns a fitted model and a table of results. Only then does it open up to show what’s inside. The course runs the same way: 1-full-pipeline.qmd assembles the whole thing once, then every page after it opens up one piece.
That’s deliberate. R functions like recipe(), mutate(), and tune() name what they do closely enough that someone with limited R experience can run the pipeline and follow its logic, even before they could write any of it themselves. Only later does peeling back a layer become worth the time. Every page that unpacks a function names its source file. Digging further is always one open file and the R console away.
R for Data Science covers the R foundations this course assumes, or skips past to keep moving. The Posit cheatsheets cover most packages this course uses, in a page or two each. If you want to understand R as a language, not just this pipeline, start with the Foundations section of Advanced R. Finally, the Tidy Modeling with R book proposes a deep dive into the Tidymodels framework.

title: Soil mid-infrared spectroscopy
text:
The course

Getting set up: install R, Positron, and the packages this course uses.
The full pipeline: load, preprocess, tune, test, and predict, once, end to end, before any of it gets explained.
Loading spectral data: read a folder of OPUS files and a wet chemistry CSV into one tibble.
Exploratory data analysis: look at the spectra and the soil properties before modelling anything.
Feature engineering: build a recipes pipeline out of resampling, SNV, and Savitzky-Golay steps.
Outlier detection: use PCA on the preprocessed spectra to find samples a model shouldn’t trust.
Evaluating performance: split the data, fit a model, and score it with tidymodels.
Preparing OSSL: pull a working sample from the Open Soil Spectral Library.
Predicting exchangeable potassium using OSSL: the same pipeline, run end to end on a public, global dataset.

Start at Getting set up if your R environment isn’t ready yet.

Outlier detection

library(here)
library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(skimr)
source(here("R", "prepare_data.R"))
source(here("R", "steps.R"))
source(here("R", "plots.R"))
theme_set(theme_bw())
tidymodels_prefer()
References: - recipes R package (Tidymodels)
SPECTRA_DIR = here("data/RT_spectra")
SOIL_PROP_FILE = here("data/RT_wetchem_soildata.csv")
TARGET <- "clay_perc"

# --- Preprocessing ----------------------------------------------------------
RESAMPLE_BY <- 5L
RESAMPLING_GRID <- seq(3995, 600, by = -5)
SG_W        <- 15L 
SG_P        <- 3L 
SG_M        <- 1L

title: Outlier detection
text:
Getting data

data <- prepare_rt(SPECTRA_DIR, SOIL_PROP_FILE)

title: Outlier detection
text:
Pre-processing recipe

spc_cols <- names(data)[startsWith(names(data), "wn_")]
meta_cols <- setdiff(names(data), c(TARGET, spc_cols))


rec <- recipe(data) |>
  update_role(all_of(TARGET),  new_role = "outcome") |>
  update_role(all_of(spc_cols), new_role = "predictor") |>
  update_role(all_of(meta_cols), new_role = "metadata") |> 
  step_log(all_outcomes(), base = 10) |>
  step_resample(grid = RESAMPLING_GRID) |> 
  step_snv() |> 
  step_sg(w = SG_W, p = SG_P, m = SG_M)


rec_prep <- prep(rec, training = data, verbose = TRUE)

oper 2 step resample [training] 
oper 3 step snv [training]

title: Exploratory Data Analysis

Getting data

title: Exploratory Data Analysis

Summary statistics
Three tools summarize the same tibble here. summary() is base R’s quick per-column stats. glimpse() trades full statistics for seeing every column at a glance. skimr::skim() adds missingness and a spark histogram per column, worth it once a dataset has more than a handful of properties. title: Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
Soil properties histogram

A single histogram






NoteBuilding a plot in layers



ggplot2 builds a plot in layers. ggplot() sets up the data and the mapping from columns to visual properties through aes(). Each geom_*() adds one layer: points, lines, histograms. The ggplot2 book covers every layer this course uses and plenty it doesn’t.


clay_perc’s histogram is roughly the shape you’d expect: no long tail, nothing to fix.

data |> 
    ggplot(aes(x = clay_perc)) +
    geom_histogram()








potassium_cmolkg isn’t so well-behaved. The QQ-plots below make the case properly. Log-transforming the column itself is one fix:

data |>
  mutate(potassium_cmolkg = log10(potassium_cmolkg)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = potassium_cmolkg)) +
  geom_histogram(bins=10, na.rm = TRUE)








Or transform just the axis display, keeping the original units as labels rather than the log values:

data |>
    ggplot(aes(x = potassium_cmolkg)) +
    geom_histogram(bins=10) +
    scale_x_log10()










All soil properties
This generalizes the same log-scaled view to every property at once. pH_H20 is left out. It’s already a log scale. Logging it again would make its skew worse, not better.

soil_long <- data |> 
  select(!starts_with("wn_")) |>
  pivot_longer(
    where(is.numeric),
    names_to = "soil_prop",
    values_to = "value"
  )


soil_long |> 
  filter(soil_prop != "pH_H20") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins=10) +
  facet_wrap(~soil_prop, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_x_log10()

title: Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
Soil properties QQ-plots
A QQ plot checks a variable against a normal distribution. Points that follow the diagonal line come from something close to normal. Points that curve away from it don’t.

soil_long |> 
  ggplot(aes(sample = value)) +
  stat_qq(na.rm = TRUE) +
  stat_qq_line(na.rm = TRUE) +
  facet_wrap(~soil_prop, scales = "free")








carbon_org_perc and carbon_tot_perc curve furthest from the line, the same properties 2-loading-data.qmd flagged potassium_cmolkg for, only more so. Log-transforming pulls most of them back toward it:

soil_long |> 
  filter(value > 0) |>
  mutate(log_value = log(value)) |>
  ggplot(aes(sample = log_value)) +
  stat_qq(na.rm = TRUE) +
  stat_qq_line(na.rm = TRUE) +
  facet_wrap(~soil_prop, scales = "free")








carbon_org_perc makes the clearest case. Its raw skewness is 6.4, against 2.3 for potassium_cmolkg. Log-transformed, that drops to 0.1. The range runs from 0.08% to 49%, a roughly 600-fold spread across 69 samples. Three reasons favor fitting a model on log10(carbon_org_perc) instead of the raw value.
A model fit on the raw scale can predict a negative carbon percentage. Back-transforming a log-scale prediction with 10^y never can.
Squared-error loss on the raw scale weighs every percentage point of error the same, wherever it falls on the scale. That lets the handful of high-carbon samples dominate the loss, since their absolute errors are bigger. On the log scale, the same absolute error costs more for a low-carbon sample than a high one. The model can’t just chase the few high values at the expense of everyone else.
Skewed variables like this one also tend to have variance that grows with the value. Most classical inference tools assume that variance stays constant across the range. The log transform tends to even it out.
There’s a cost too. Coefficients and metrics like RMSE come back in log units, not percent carbon. Reading them in the original units takes a deliberate back-transform.

title: Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
Soil properties correlation
Organic carbon and phosphorus correlate on the log scale: r = 0.40 (p = 0.018, n = 34, using only samples with both measured). It isn’t a tight relationship. Soils richer in organic matter tend to hold more phosphorus too.

data |>
  filter(carbon_org_perc > 0, phosporus_mgkg > 0) |>
  ggplot(aes(
    x = carbon_org_perc,
    y = phosporus_mgkg
  )) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(
    x = "Organic carbon (%)",
    y = "Phosphorus (mg/kg)"
  )

title: Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
Spectra

All spectra

data |> plot_spectra()










Unpacking plot_spectra()
plot_spectra() reshapes the wavenumber columns into long format, then builds the plot below in stages. Colouring every one of the 70 samples by ID, the first attempt, produces a legend nobody can read:

spectra <- data |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("wn_"),
    names_to = "wavenumber",
    names_prefix = "wn_",
    names_transform = list(wavenumber = as.numeric),
    values_to = "absorbance"
  )


ggplot(spectra, aes(wavenumber, absorbance, group = smp_id, colour = smp_id)) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_x_reverse() +
  labs(
    x = "Wavenumber",
    y = "Absorbance",
    colour = "Sample"
  ) +
  theme_bw()








Dropping the per-sample colour and blending lines with alpha instead makes the overall shape visible:

ggplot(spectra, aes(wavenumber, absorbance, group = smp_id)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.35, colour = "steelblue") +
  scale_x_reverse() +
  theme_bw()








Tidying the axis breaks and labels gets to what plot_spectra() actually returns:

ggplot(spectra, aes(wavenumber, absorbance, group = smp_id)) +
    geom_line(alpha = 0.35, colour = "steelblue") +
    scale_x_reverse(
        breaks = seq(500, 4000, by = 250),
        minor_breaks = seq(500, 4000, by = 125)) +
    labs(
        x = "Wavenumber (cm-1)",
        y = "Absorbance",
        colour = "Sample") +
    theme_bw()










Colouring by organic carbon
Mean absorbance across the whole spectrum correlates weakly with organic carbon: r = 0.32, p = 0.007. Higher-carbon samples sit a little higher on the y-axis overall. Colouring by carbon_org_perc makes that pattern visible directly on the spectra:

ggplot(
  spectra,
  aes(
    x = wavenumber,
    y = absorbance,
    group = smp_id,
    colour = carbon_org_perc
  )
) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.5) +
  scale_x_reverse(
    breaks = seq(500, 4000, by = 250),
    minor_breaks = seq(500, 4000, by = 125)
  ) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(
    name = "Organic carbon (%)",
    na.value = "grey70"
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Wavenumber (cm⁻¹)",
    y = "Absorbance"
  )










Grouping by carbon quartile
This splits the same idea into four groups instead of a continuous gradient, easier to compare by eye than shades of one colour:

spectra_grouped <- spectra |>
  filter(!is.na(carbon_org_perc)) |>
  mutate(
    carbon_group = ntile(carbon_org_perc, 4),
    carbon_group = factor(
      carbon_group,
      labels = c("Lowest", "Low–middle", "High–middle", "Highest")
    )
  )


ggplot(
  spectra_grouped,
  aes(wavenumber, absorbance, group = smp_id)
) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.35, colour = "steelblue") +
  facet_wrap(~ carbon_group) +
  scale_x_reverse() +
  labs(
    x = "Wavenumber (cm⁻¹)",
    y = "Absorbance",
    title = "Spectra grouped by organic carbon"
  )










Zooming into a wavenumber range
This shows the full spectrum again, immediately before zooming in on 2200–2700 cm⁻¹. That’s a comparatively flat stretch. Mean absorbance there runs lower and less variable across samples (1.31, sd 0.14) than the spectrum as a whole (1.72, sd 0.17). coord_cartesian() crops the view without dropping any data, unlike setting axis limits directly.

spectra_no_na <- spectra |>
  filter(!is.na(carbon_org_perc))


ggplot(
  spectra_no_na,
  aes(wavenumber, absorbance, group = smp_id)
) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.35, colour = "steelblue") +
  scale_x_reverse(
    breaks = seq(500, 4000, by = 250),
    minor_breaks = seq(500, 4000, by = 125)
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Wavenumber (cm⁻¹)",
    y = "Absorbance"
  ) +
  theme_bw()









ggplot(
  spectra_no_na,
  aes(wavenumber, absorbance, group = smp_id)
) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.35, colour = "steelblue") +
  scale_x_reverse(
    breaks = seq(2200, 2700, by = 100),
    minor_breaks = seq(2200, 2700, by = 50)
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(2700, 2200)) +
  labs(
    x = "Wavenumber (cm⁻¹)",
    y = "Absorbance"
  ) +
  theme_bw()

title: The full pipeline
text:
This page runs the whole pipeline once, start to finish: load spectra, preprocess them, tune and fit a model, test it, predict with it. Every step below gets its own full page later in the course. This page exists to show the shape of the whole thing before any of that detail.
The ring trial (RT) samples used throughout this course come from a real interlaboratory study: labs in several countries, including the IAEA’s, scanned the same soil samples on their own instruments, to see how much spectra disagree from lab to lab. Safanelli et al. (2023) covers what came out of it. I’m one of its authors.

# --- Config ------------------------------------------------------------------
library(here)
library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(plsmod)
source(here("R", "prepare_data.R"))
source(here("R", "steps.R"))
source(here("R", "split.R"))
tidymodels_prefer()

SPECTRA_DIR = here("data/RT_spectra")
SOIL_PROP_FILE = here("data/RT_wetchem_soildata.csv")
TARGET <- "carbon_tot_perc"
RESAMPLING_GRID <- seq(3995, 600, by = -5)


# --- Loading ------------------------------------------------------------------
# RT_44 dropped as a known outlier -> 5-outlier-detection.qmd
data <- prepare_rt(SPECTRA_DIR, SOIL_PROP_FILE) |> filter(smp_id != "RT_44")


# --- Preprocessing --------------------------------------------------------------
# log-scale, resample, SNV, Savitzky-Golay -> 4-feature-engineering.qmd
spc_cols <- names(data)[startsWith(names(data), "wn_")]
meta_cols <- setdiff(names(data), c(TARGET, spc_cols))

rec <- recipe(data) |>
  update_role(all_of(TARGET), new_role = "outcome") |>
  update_role(all_of(spc_cols), new_role = "predictor") |>
  update_role(all_of(meta_cols), new_role = "metadata") |>
  step_log(all_outcomes(), base = 10) |>
  step_resample(grid = RESAMPLING_GRID) |>
  step_snv() |>
  step_sg(w = 15L, p = 3L, m = 1L)

# --- Tuning -----------------------------------------------------------------------
# search num_comp, pick the best, lock it in -> 6-evaluating-performance.qmd
split <- kennard_stone_split(data, prop = 50/70, cols = starts_with("wn_"))
folds <- vfold_cv(training(split), v = 10, repeats = 10, strata = TARGET, breaks = 2)

wf <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(rec) |>
  add_model(pls(num_comp = tune()) |> set_engine("mixOmics") |> set_mode("regression"))

tune_res <- tune_grid(wf, resamples = folds, grid = tibble(num_comp = 2:20))
best <- select_best(tune_res, metric = "rmse")
final_wf <- wf |> finalize_workflow(best)

# --- Testing ------------------------------------------------------------------------
# fit on train, score once on the held-out test split
final_res <- final_wf |> last_fit(split)
collect_metrics(final_res) |> select(.metric, .estimate)

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  .metric .estimate
  <chr>       <dbl>
1 rmse        0.131
2 rsq         0.933

# --- Predicting ---------------------------------------------------------------------
# .pred and TARGET are both log10 here -> 2-loading-data.qmd, 3-eda.qmd
collect_predictions(final_res) |> 
  select(all_of(TARGET), .pred) |>
  head()

# A tibble: 6 × 2
  carbon_tot_perc   .pred
            <dbl>   <dbl>
1          0.296  0.322  
2          0.332  0.306  
3          0.311  0.320  
4          0.318  0.308  
5          0.258  0.254  
6          0.0192 0.00379






References

Safanelli, José L. et al. 2023. “An Interlaboratory Comparison of Mid-Infrared Spectra Acquisition: Instruments and Procedures Matter.” Geoderma 440: 116724. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.geoderma.2023.116724.

title: Getting set up
text:
Install Positron
Download Positron and install it.
Both Positron and RStudio are built by Posit, but only Positron keeps getting new features. RStudio keeps stability, security and bug-fix updates. Positron is built on the same open-source foundation as VS Code and runs R and Python side by side in one place. For anyone here who already works in Python day to day, the same editor covers both languages.
Once Positron is installed, open it and check it has found your R installation: bottom status bar -> interpreter picker, or Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+P -> “R: Select Interpreter”.

title: Getting set up
text:
Get the course materials
Go to the course repository on GitHub, click Code -> Download ZIP, then unzip it. Open the unzipped folder in Positron (File -> Open Folder…).
If you already use git day to day, cloning works just as well:


Terminal

git clone https://github.com/franckalbinet/tidy-mirs.git

title: Getting set up
text:
Install the R packages
This project uses renv to pin exact package versions, the same idea as Python’s venv or conda. It gives you a project-local library instead of your regular R install. renv.lock records exactly what’s installed. Everyone in the course runs the same versions we tested against.
Open the project in Positron and run, in the R console:


Console

renv::restore()

The first run downloads and installs everything listed in renv.lock into a project-local library. It can take a few minutes and, on some platforms, needs to compile a couple of packages from source. It touches nothing outside this project folder.
renv::restore() can fail behind a restrictive network proxy, on a locked-down institutional laptop, or in similar cases. If it does, install the same packages directly into your regular R library instead:


Console

install.packages(c(
  "tidyverse", "tidymodels", "here", "opusreader2",
  "skimr", "plsmod", "prospectr", "resemble", "hexbin", "glue"
))

install.packages("BiocManager")
BiocManager::install("mixOmics")

This gets you everything you need for the course. It isn’t version-pinned. Let us know if something behaves differently from the demo.

title: Loading spectral data
text:
1-full-pipeline.qmd already called prepare_rt() once, to get moving. This page opens that call up. It loads spectra and soil chemistry for this dataset’s soil samples. It turns them into the single tibble every later page in this course starts from. source() runs a plain R script and adds what it defines to your session, the job import does in Python. read_opus_tbl() and prepare_rt(), the two functions this page uses, live in R/io.R and R/prepare_data.R.
library(here)
library(tidyverse)
source(here("R", "io.R"))
source(here("R", "prepare_data.R"))
Two paths to set: the folder holding the OPUS files the spectrometer wrote, and the CSV holding the wet chemistry measured on the same samples.
SPECTRA_DIR = here("data/RT_spectra")
SOIL_PROP_FILE = here("data/RT_wetchem_soildata.csv")

title: Loading spectral data
section: Loading and joining everything in one call

Loading and joining everything in one call

title: Loading spectral data
text:
Unpacking prepare_rt()
The rest of this page opens up what prepare_rt() does underneath, one step at a time. Open R/prepare_data.R alongside this page if you want to follow the source directly. Each step below matches one chunk of that function.

Reading OPUS spectra files
The lab’s Bruker instrument writes one OPUS binary file per scan, with a .0 extension: RT_01_001.0, RT_01_002.0, and so on for each of the four repeat scans per sample. read_opus_tbl() reads every file in a folder and returns one row per scan, wavenumbers as columns.

spectra <- read_opus_tbl(SPECTRA_DIR)
spectra

Averaging replicate scans
Each sample was scanned four times. read_opus_tbl() keeps every scan as its own row. str_extract() pulls the shared sample ID out of each scan’s filename, for example RT_01 out of RT_01_001. Grouping by that ID and averaging every wavenumber column collapses the four scans into the one row per sample the rest of the pipeline needs.






Notedplyr, four verbs at a time



This chunk is your first look at dplyr, the package tidyverse uses for reshaping tables like this one. mutate() adds a column, group_by() marks rows to summarize together, summarize() collapses each group to one row, and across() applies the same function to several columns at once, here every column starting wn_. These four verbs cover most day-to-day data wrangling in R. The dplyr cheatsheet and the dplyr reference site cover the rest.



spectra_mean <- spectra |>
    mutate(smp_id = str_extract(spc_id, "RT_\\d+")) |>
    group_by(smp_id) |>
    summarize(across(starts_with("wn_"), mean))



Loading soil properties
The wet chemistry lives in a plain CSV, one row per sample.

soil_prop <- read_csv(SOIL_PROP_FILE)

Interactively (e.g. in Positron or RStudio), view(soil_prop) opens the data viewer pane. For a rendered page, printing the tibble works just as well here. It has a manageable number of columns to show inline.

    left_join(soil_prop, by = c("smp_id" = "sample_id"))

title: Loading spectral data
text:
Digging further
prepare_rt() in R/prepare_data.R is exactly the four chunks above, chained. To see how read_opus_tbl() itself gets from a folder of .0 files to a tibble, open R/io.R and step through it in the R console: build a small path, run read_opus(dsn = path) from opusreader2 on its own, inspect what comes back, then run each following line by hand. These scripts aren’t a package. ?read_opus_tbl won’t find a help page. The roxygen comment above each function is written in the same format a package help page would show, and reads the same way top to bottom.

title: Features engineering
text:
library(here)
library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(skimr)
source(here("R", "prepare_data.R"))
source(here("R", "steps.R"))
source(here("R", "plots.R"))
theme_set(theme_bw())
tidymodels_prefer()
SPECTRA_DIR = here("data/RT_spectra")
SOIL_PROP_FILE = here("data/RT_wetchem_soildata.csv")
TARGET <- "potassium_cmolkg"

# --- Preprocessing ----------------------------------------------------------
RESAMPLE_BY <- 5L
RESAMPLING_GRID <- seq(3995, 600, by = -5)
SG_W        <- 15L
SG_P        <- 3L
SG_M        <- 1L

title: Features engineering
text:
Getting data

data <- prepare_rt(SPECTRA_DIR, SOIL_PROP_FILE)

title: Features engineering
text:
Recipes
1-full-pipeline.qmd already built and used a recipe once, without explaining it. This page is that explanation. A recipe in tidymodels is a specification of preprocessing steps, written once and reused everywhere a model needs data in the same shape. The recipes package and the tidymodels recipes guide cover the general vocabulary this page assumes, alongside the Posit cheatsheets already pointed to from the course homepage.
Base recipes ships steps for the usual tabular preprocessing, centring, scaling, dummy variables, but nothing for a spectrum. step_snv(), step_sg(), and step_resample(), defined in R/steps.R, close that gap.
Each one wraps a prospectr or resemble function, prospectr::standardNormalVariate(), prospectr::savitzkyGolay(), prospectr::resample(), inside the contract a recipes step needs: a constructor, prep(), bake(), print(), tidy(). That’s what lets step_snv() sit in a recipe next to step_log() or any other tidymodels step. It gets ordered, tuned, and applied the same way every other step does.

Defining roles
Every column in data gets a role before any preprocessing happens: potassium_cmolkg as the outcome, the wn_* columns as predictors, everything else, sample_id, source, the other soil properties, as metadata. Metadata columns ride along through the whole recipe unchanged. They’re not used to fit anything, but having them still attached to data_processed later makes it possible to check whether prediction errors line up with, say, clay content or sample source, without a separate join back to the original data.

spc_cols <- names(data)[startsWith(names(data), "wn_")]
meta_cols <- setdiff(names(data), c(TARGET, spc_cols))

rec <- recipe(data) |>
  update_role(all_of(TARGET),  new_role = "outcome") |>
  update_role(all_of(spc_cols), new_role = "predictor") |>
  update_role(all_of(meta_cols), new_role = "metadata")


summary(rec)

# A tibble: 1,715 × 4
   variable  type      role      source  
   <chr>     <list>    <chr>     <chr>   
 1 smp_id    <chr [3]> metadata  original
 2 wn_3997.5 <chr [2]> predictor original
 3 wn_3995.5 <chr [2]> predictor original
 4 wn_3993.4 <chr [2]> predictor original
 5 wn_3991.4 <chr [2]> predictor original
 6 wn_3989.3 <chr [2]> predictor original
 7 wn_3987.3 <chr [2]> predictor original
 8 wn_3985.2 <chr [2]> predictor original
 9 wn_3983.2 <chr [2]> predictor original
10 wn_3981.1 <chr [2]> predictor original
# ℹ 1,705 more rows




All steps together
This shows the full preprocessing chain at once: log-scaling the outcome, resampling the spectral grid, SNV, then Savitzky-Golay. The rest of this page unpacks these steps one by one, adding one more each time.

rec_all <- recipe(data) |>
  update_role(all_of(TARGET),  new_role = "outcome") |>
  update_role(all_of(spc_cols), new_role = "predictor") |>
  update_role(all_of(meta_cols), new_role = "metadata") |> 
  step_log(all_outcomes(), base = 10) |>
  step_resample(grid = RESAMPLING_GRID) |> 
  step_snv() |> 
  step_sg(w = SG_W, p = SG_P, m = SG_M)


rec_prep <- prep(rec_all, training = data, verbose = TRUE)

oper 1 step log [training] 
oper 2 step resample [training] 
oper 3 step snv [training] 
oper 4 step sg [training] 
The retained training set is ~ 0.44 Mb  in memory.

data_processed <- bake(
  rec_prep,
  new_data = NULL
)


data_processed |> plot_spectra()

title: Features engineering
text:
Unpacking the recipe
The rest of this page adds one step at a time to rec. Each one’s effect on the spectra is visible on its own this way. Every version gets prep()ped then bake()d before plotting.
prep() is where a step learns anything it needs from the training data, a column’s mean and standard deviation for centring and scaling, say. bake() is where that learned information gets applied: to the training data here, to a validation or test set later, using the exact same numbers either time.
None of the three steps below actually estimate anything from the training set as a whole. SNV and Savitzky-Golay both act one row at a time, using only that row’s own values. Resampling only depends on the wavenumber grid, not on any sample’s measurements. prep() still runs before each one, mostly resolving which columns it applies to. The training/test separation it exists for matters most once a step needs to remember something computed across rows, a column mean for centring, say, rather than something computed within each row.

Resampling
This step does two things. step_log(all_outcomes(), base = 10) log-scales the outcome, the fix for potassium_cmolkg’s skew discussed back in 2-loading-data.qmd and 3-eda.qmd. step_resample() interpolates every spectrum onto RESAMPLING_GRID, an evenly spaced set of wavenumbers 5 cm⁻¹ apart, versus the roughly 2 cm⁻¹ spacing read_opus_tbl() returns. That cuts the predictor count from 1707 columns to 680. It also guarantees every sample lands on the same wavenumber axis, even where the source instrument didn’t.

rec_res <- rec |>
  step_log(all_outcomes(), base = 10) |>
  step_resample(grid = RESAMPLING_GRID)


rec_prep <- prep(rec_res, training = data, verbose = TRUE)

oper 1 step log [training] 
oper 2 step resample [training] 
The retained training set is ~ 0.45 Mb  in memory.

data_processed <- bake(
  rec_prep,
  new_data = NULL
)


data_processed |> plot_spectra()










SNV
step_snv() centres and scales each spectrum by its own mean and standard deviation, row by row, not column by column. That corrects for scatter effects, differences in particle size or packing that shift a whole spectrum up or down without changing its shape. Two spectra with the same underlying chemistry but different scatter come out looking the same after SNV. Two spectra with genuinely different chemistry stay different.

rec_snv <- rec |>
  step_log(all_outcomes(), base = 10) |>
  step_resample(grid = RESAMPLING_GRID) |>
  step_snv()


rec_prep <- prep(rec_snv, training = data, verbose = TRUE)

oper 1 step log [training] 
oper 2 step resample [training] 
oper 3 step snv [training] 
The retained training set is ~ 0.45 Mb  in memory.

data_processed <- bake(
  rec_prep,
  new_data = NULL
)


data_processed |> plot_spectra()










Savitzky-Golay
step_sg() fits a polynomial of order SG_P inside a moving window SG_W wavenumbers wide, centred on each point. It then reads off either a smoothed value or a derivative from that fit, depending on SG_M. With SG_M = 1 here, each spectrum gets its first derivative instead of a smoothed value. A first derivative removes baseline shifts entirely, rather than just correcting for them the way SNV does. It also tends to sharpen overlapping peaks.
Smoothing and differentiating both cost some data at the edges. prospectr::savitzkyGolay() trims (w - 1) / 2 wavenumbers off each end. That’s why the plotted spectrum below is narrower than the one above it.
SG_W = 15, SG_P = 3, and SG_M = 1 are sensible defaults here, tuned by eye on a dataset rather than picked arbitrarily. Tuning them properly, as part of a model fit, comes later in this course.

rec_sg <- rec |>
  step_log(all_outcomes(), base = 10) |>
  step_resample(grid = RESAMPLING_GRID) |> 
  step_snv() |> 
  step_sg(w = SG_W, p = SG_P, m = SG_M)


rec_prep <- prep(rec_sg, training = data, verbose = TRUE)

oper 1 step log [training] 
oper 2 step resample [training] 
oper 3 step snv [training] 
oper 4 step sg [training] 
The retained training set is ~ 0.44 Mb  in memory.

data_processed <- bake(
  rec_prep,
  new_data = NULL
)


data_processed |> plot_spectra()

title: Evaluating performance
text:
1-full-pipeline.qmd already tuned this same model on this same data. It picked a number of components with select_best(). This page runs the same tuning in more depth: the CV curve behind that choice, and select_by_one_std_err() as a simpler alternative to picking the single best value.
library(here)
library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(skimr)
library(plsmod)
source(here("R", "prepare_data.R"))
source(here("R", "steps.R"))
source(here("R", "split.R"))
theme_set(theme_bw())
tidymodels_prefer()
SPECTRA_DIR = here("data/RT_spectra")
SOIL_PROP_FILE = here("data/RT_wetchem_soildata.csv")
TARGET <- "carbon_tot_perc"

# --- Preprocessing ----------------------------------------------------------
RESAMPLE_BY <- 5L
RESAMPLING_GRID <- seq(3995, 600, by = -5)
SG_W        <- 15L   
SG_P        <- 3L    
SG_M        <- 1L

title: Evaluating performance
text:
Getting data

data <- prepare_rt(SPECTRA_DIR, SOIL_PROP_FILE)|> filter(smp_id != "RT_44")


split <- kennard_stone_split(data, prop = 50/70, cols = starts_with("wn_"))

# or
# split <- initial_split(data, prop = 50/70)


set.seed(123)

folds <- vfold_cv(
  training(split),
  v = 10,
  repeats = 10,
  strata = TARGET,
  breaks = 2
)


spc_cols <- names(data)[startsWith(names(data), "wn_")]
meta_cols <- setdiff(names(data), c(TARGET, spc_cols))

rec <- recipe(data) |>
  update_role(all_of(TARGET),  new_role = "outcome") |>
  update_role(all_of(spc_cols), new_role = "predictor") |>
  update_role(all_of(meta_cols), new_role = "metadata") |> 
  step_log(all_outcomes(), base = 10) |>
  step_resample(grid = RESAMPLING_GRID) |> 
  step_snv() |> 
  step_sg(w = SG_W, p = SG_P, m = SG_M)


pls_spec <- pls(num_comp = tune()) |>
  set_engine("mixOmics") |>
  set_mode("regression")


wf <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(rec) |>
  add_model(pls_spec)


num_comp_grid <- tibble(num_comp = 2:20)


tune_res <- tune_grid(
  wf,
  resamples = folds,
  grid = num_comp_grid
)


collect_metrics(tune_res)

10        6 rsq     standard   0.927   100 0.00724 pre0_mod05_post0
# ℹ 28 more rows



autoplot(tune_res)









collect_metrics(tune_res) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = num_comp, y = mean)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean - std_err, ymax = mean + std_err), width = 0.1, color = "grey20", linetype = "22") +
  geom_point(size=1.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ .metric, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Number of PLS components", y = NULL,
       title = "CV performance vs number of PLS components")









best_rmse <- select_best(tune_res, metric = "rmse")
best_rmse

final_wf <- wf |> finalize_workflow(best_1se)

final_res <- final_wf |> last_fit(split)


collect_metrics(final_res)
